$$ -\zeta\upvarphi_{R}^{\prime}\frac{\partial R}{\partial t}=-\nabla^{2}\Sigma_{rr}+\frac{2}{r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{G}}{\partial r}+\frac{2}{r^{2}}\mathcal{G}-\zeta\bm{\nabla}\cdot\bm{\eta}^{\rm act}, $$

where $\upvarphi_{R}^{\prime}$ is the $r$ derivative of $\upvarphi_{R}$ . We now define the inverse Laplace operator as:

$$ \nabla^{-2}f(r)=-\int_{r}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{r_{2}}\text{d}r_{2}\text{d}r_{1}\left(\frac{r_{1}}{r_{2}}\right)^{2}f(r_{1}), $$

where $f(r)$ is a function that vanishes in the limit of $r\to\infty$ . We apply the inverse Laplace operator to both sides of Eq. (2.4). The effect of the inverse Laplace operator on the second term on the left hand side is:

$$ \nabla^{-2}\left[\frac{2}{r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{G}}{\partial r}\right]=-\int_{r}^{\infty}\text{d}r_{2}\frac{1}{r_{2}^{2}}\int_{0}^{r_{2}}\text{d}r_{1}2r_{1}\frac{\partial\mathcal{G}}{\partial r_{1}}. $$

We now integrate Eq. (2.6) by parts while choosing:

$$ \displaystyle u=\int_{0}^{r_{2}}\text{d}r_{1}2r_{1}\frac{\partial\mathcal{G}}{\partial r_{1}} \displaystyle,\quad du=2r_{2}\frac{\partial\mathcal{G}}{\partial r_{2}}\text{d}r_{2}, \displaystyle dv=-\frac{1}{r_{2}^{2}}\text{d}r_{2} \displaystyle,\quad v=\frac{1}{r_{2}}. $$

Then Eq. (2.6) can equivalently be expressed as

$$ \nabla^{-2}\left[\frac{2}{r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{G}}{\partial r}\right]=-\frac{2}{r}\int_{0}^{r}\text{d}r_{1}r_{1}\frac{\partial\mathcal{G}}{\partial r_{1}}+2\mathcal{G}(r). $$

A second integration by parts results in:

$$ \displaystyle\nabla^{-2}\left[\frac{2}{r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{G}}{\partial r}\right] \displaystyle=-\frac{2}{r}\left(r\mathcal{G}(r)-\int_{0}^{r}\mathcal{G}\text{d}r_{1}\right)+2\mathcal{G}(r), \displaystyle=\frac{2}{r}\int_{0}^{r}\mathcal{G}\text{d}r_{1}. $$

Applying a similar procedure to the other terms in Eq. (2.4) results in:

$$ \nabla^{-2}\left[\frac{2}{r^{2}}\mathcal{G}\right]=-\frac{2}{r}\int_{0}^{r}\mathcal{G}\text{d}r_{1}-2\int_{r}^{\infty}\frac{\mathcal{G}}{r_{1}}\text{d}r_{1}, $$

$$ \nabla^{-2}\left[-\zeta\upvarphi^{\prime}_{R}\frac{\partial R}{\partial t}\right]=\zeta R\frac{\partial R}{\partial t}\left(\rho^{\rm sat}-\rho^{\rm in}\right)+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{R}\right), $$

$$ \nabla^{-2}\left[-\nabla^{2}\Sigma_{rr}\right]=-\Sigma_{rr}-\mathcal{P}(\rho^{\rm sat}), $$

where the $\mathcal{P}(\rho^{\rm sat})$ in Eq. (2.11) comes from the boundary term of $\Sigma_{rr}$ as $r\to\infty$ . From the above equations one can see that applying the inverse Laplace operator to both sides of Eq. (2.4) results in:

$$ \zeta R\frac{\partial R}{\partial t}\Delta\rho+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{R}\right)=\Sigma_{rr}+\mathcal{P}(\rho^{\rm sat})+\int_{r}^{\infty}\text{d}r_{1}\frac{2}{r_{1}}\mathcal{G}-\nabla^{-2}\left[\zeta\bm{\nabla}\cdot\bm{\eta}^{\rm act}\right], $$

where we have defined the difference between an arbitrary property $a$ at the interior and exterior of the bubble/droplet as $\Delta a\equiv a^{\rm in}-a^{\rm sat}$ . We now multiply both sides of the equation by $\partial\mathcal{E}/\partial r$ and integrate from $r=0$ to $r=\infty$ :

$$ \displaystyle-\zeta R\frac{\partial R}{\partial t}\Delta\rho\Delta\mathcal{E}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{R}\right)= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\Sigma_{rr}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\text{d}r+\mathcal{P}(\rho^{\rm sat})\left(\mathcal{E}^{\rm sat}-\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}\right) \displaystyle+\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\int_{r}^{\infty}\text{d}r_{1}\frac{2\mathcal{G}}{r_{1}}-\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\nabla^{-2}\left[\zeta\bm{\nabla}\cdot\bm{\eta}^{\rm act}\right]. $$

The double integral can be integrating by parts with:

$$ \displaystyle u=\int_{r}^{\infty}\frac{2\mathcal{G}}{r_{2}}\text{d}r_{1} \displaystyle,\quad du=-\frac{2\mathcal{G}}{r}\text{d}r, \displaystyle dv=\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\text{d}r \displaystyle,\quad v=\mathcal{E} $$

$$ \displaystyle-\zeta R\frac{\partial R}{\partial t}\Delta\rho\Delta\mathcal{E}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{R}\right)= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\Sigma_{rr}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\text{d}r+\mathcal{P}(\rho^{\rm sat})\left(\mathcal{E}^{\rm sat}-\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}\right)-\frac{2\upgamma_{\rm mech}}{R}\mathcal{E}^{\rm in} \displaystyle+\frac{2}{R}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathcal{E}\mathcal{G}\text{d}r-\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\nabla^{-2}\left[\zeta\bm{\nabla}\cdot\bm{\eta}^{\rm act}\right]. $$

Now consider the first integral on the right hand side. Substituting in the constitutive expression for $\Sigma_{rr}$ from Eq. (1.6) and integrating by parts results in

$$ \int_{0}^{\infty}\Sigma_{rr}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\text{d}r=-\int_{\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}}^{\mathcal{E}^{\rm sat}}\text{d}\mathcal{E}\mathcal{P}(\rho)+\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{2}{r}a(\rho)\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial\rho}\left(\upvarphi^{\prime}_{R}\right)^{2}. $$

Substitution of Eq. (2.15) into Eq. (2.14) gives:

$$ \displaystyle-\zeta R\frac{\partial R}{\partial t}\Delta\rho\Delta\mathcal{E}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{R}\right)= \displaystyle-\int_{\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}}^{\mathcal{E}^{\rm sat}}\text{d}\mathcal{E}\mathcal{P}(\rho)+\mathcal{P}(\rho^{\rm sat})\left(\mathcal{E}^{\rm sat}-\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}\right)-\frac{2\upgamma_{\rm mech}}{R}\mathcal{E}^{\rm in} \displaystyle+\frac{2}{R}\int_{0}^{\infty}\left(\mathcal{E}\mathcal{G}+a(\rho)\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial\rho}\left(\frac{\partial\upvarphi_{R}}{\partial r}\right)^{2}\right)\text{d}r \displaystyle-\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\nabla^{-2}\left[\zeta\bm{\nabla}\cdot\bm{\eta}^{\rm act}\right]. $$

From Eq. (1.23) we can rewrite Eq. (2.16) as:

$$ \displaystyle-\zeta R\frac{\partial R}{\partial t}\Delta\rho\Delta\mathcal{E}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{R}\right)= \displaystyle-\int_{\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}}^{\mathcal{E}^{\rm sat}}\text{d}\mathcal{E}\left[\mathcal{P}(\rho)-\mathcal{P}(\rho^{\rm sat})\right]+\frac{2\upgamma_{\rm ost}}{R}\frac{\rho^{\rm sat}\Delta\mathcal{E}}{\Delta\rho} \displaystyle-\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\nabla^{-2}\left[\zeta\bm{\nabla}\cdot\bm{\eta}^{\rm act}\right]. $$

Recognizing that the first integral on the right-hand-side of Eq. (2.17) is a constant, we can rearrange:

$$ \displaystyle\zeta R\frac{\partial R}{\partial t}\Delta\rho\Delta\mathcal{E}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{R}\right)=\frac{2\upgamma_{\rm ost}\rho^{\rm sat}\Delta\mathcal{E}}{\Delta\rho}\left[\frac{1}{R_{C}}-\frac{1}{R}\right]+\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\nabla^{-2}\left[\zeta\bm{\nabla}\cdot\bm{\eta}^{\rm act}\right], $$

where the critical radius is defined as:

$$ R_{C}=\frac{2\upgamma_{\rm ost}\rho^{\rm sat}\Delta\mathcal{E}}{\Delta\rho\int_{\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}}^{\mathcal{E}^{\rm sat}}\left[\mathcal{P}(\rho)-\mathcal{P}(\rho^{\rm sat})\right]\text{d}\mathcal{E}}, $$

which is identical to the critical radius found in Section 1.1 [see Eq. (1.24)], highlighting the consistency of the two approaches.

The final evolution equation for the radial growth can be compactly written as:

$$ \zeta_{\rm eff}\frac{\partial R}{\partial t}=F^{D}(R)+\tilde{\chi}(t), $$

where we have defined an effective drag force:

$$ \zeta_{\rm eff}=\frac{4\pi\left(\rho^{\rm sat}-\rho^{\rm in}\right)^{2}R^{3}\zeta}{\rho^{\rm sat}}, $$

as well as a deterministic force:

$$ F^{D}(R)=8\pi R^{2}\upgamma_{\rm ost}\left[\frac{1}{R_{C}}-\frac{1}{R}\right]. $$

$\tilde{\chi}(t)$ represents the stochastic force with:

$$ \tilde{\chi}(t)=\frac{\zeta_{\rm eff}}{R\Delta\rho\Delta\mathcal{E}}\nabla^{-2}\left[\bm{\nabla}\cdot\bm{\eta}^{\rm act}\right]. $$

In Section 2.2, we derive the statistics of $\tilde{\chi}(t)$ finding that it has zero mean and a variance given by:

$$ \langle\tilde{\chi}(t)\tilde{\chi}(t^{\prime})\rangle=2k_{B}T^{\rm act}\zeta_{\rm eff}\delta(t-t^{\prime}). $$

From Eqs. (2.20) and (2.24) we can see that the dynamics of the nucleus obey the fluctuation dissipation theorem. In addition, the deterministic term can be integrated to define an effective potential governing nucleation as further discussed in Section 2.3.

### 2.2 Noise Statistics

We now seek to derive the statistics of $\tilde{\chi}(t)$ [Eq. (2.24)]. We start by rewriting the statistics of $\bm{\eta}^{\rm act}$ [Eq. (2.1c)] to be compatible with our spherical symmetry conditions:

$$ \langle\bm{\eta}^{\rm act}(\mathbf{r},t)\bm{\eta}^{\rm act}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime},t^{\prime})\rangle=2\frac{k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\left(\rho\mathbf{I}-\frac{d}{d-1}\mathbf{Q}^{\prime}\right)\delta(t-t^{\prime})\left(\frac{\delta(r-r^{\prime})}{r^{2}}\right). $$

As found in Ref. [21], $\mathbf{Q}^{\prime}$ is given by:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{Q}^{\prime}=-\frac{d-1}{\ell_{o}^{2}D_{R}\zeta\overline{U}(\rho)}\left[\kappa_{1}(\rho)\nabla^{2}\rho\mathbf{I}+\kappa_{3}(\rho)\bm{\nabla}\rho\bm{\nabla}\rho\right]. $$

Thus, $\bm{\eta}^{\rm act}$ may have anisotropic contributions to its correlator, particularly at interfaces where gradients in the density are large. This anisotropy is due to $\bm{\eta}^{\rm act}$ ’s microscopic roots in the aggregate of individual $\bm{\Omega}_{i}\times\mathbf{q}_{i}$ . In regions of space with nematic alignment, the result of the cross product of an isotropic noise with each orientation $\mathbf{q}_{i}$ will be biased towards directions orthogonal to that alignment. Before finding the statistics of $\tilde{\chi}$ , we first find the statistics of $\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r},t)$ , which we define as

$$ \xi_{R}(\mathbf{r},t)=-\bm{\nabla}\cdot\bm{\eta}^{\rm act}. $$

We split the correlations of $\xi_{R}$ into three contributions,

$$ \langle\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r},t)\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime},t^{\prime})\rangle=\langle\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r},t)\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime},t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}+\langle\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r},t)\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime},t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm aniso}_{1}+\langle\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r},t)\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime},t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm aniso}_{2}, $$

where the contribution labeled $\rm{iso}$ originates from the component of the $\bm{\eta}^{\rm act}$ correlator proportional to $\rho\mathbf{I}$ while the contributions labeled $\rm{aniso}$ originates from the component of the $\bm{\eta}^{\rm act}$ correlator proportional to $\mathbf{Q}^{\prime}$ . Each contribution is given by:

$$ \langle\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r},t)\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime},t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}=-\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial r}+\frac{2}{r}\right)\left[\rho\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(\frac{\delta(r-r^{\prime})}{r^{2}}\right)\right], $$

$$ \displaystyle\langle\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r},t)\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime},t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm aniso}_{1}= \displaystyle-\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial r}+\frac{2}{r}\right) \displaystyle\left[\left(\frac{1}{\ell_{o}^{2}D_{R}\zeta\overline{U}}\left[\kappa_{1}(\rho)\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial r}+\frac{2}{r}\right)\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r}-\kappa_{3}(\rho)\left(\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r}\right)^{2}\right]\right)\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(\frac{\delta(r-r^{\prime})}{r^{2}}\right)\right], $$

and

$$ \langle\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r},t)\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime},t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm aniso}_{2}=\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial r}+\frac{2}{r}\right)\left[\left(\frac{1}{r^{\prime}}\frac{1}{\ell_{o}^{2}D_{R}\zeta\overline{U}}\left[\kappa_{3}(\rho)\left(\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r}\right)^{2}\right]\right)\frac{\delta(r-r^{\prime})}{r^{2}}\right]. $$

We now define $\chi(t)$ as:

$$ \chi(t)=-\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\int_{r}^{\infty}\text{d}r_{2}\frac{1}{r_{2}^{2}}\int_{0}^{r_{2}}r_{1}^{2}\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r}_{1},t). $$

The correlations of $\chi(t)$ are then given by

$$ \langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle=\left\langle\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\int_{r}^{\infty}\text{d}r_{2}\frac{1}{r_{2}^{2}}\int_{0}^{r_{2}}r_{1}^{2}\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r}_{1},t)\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}}\int_{r}^{\infty}\text{d}r_{4}\frac{1}{r_{4}^{2}}\int_{0}^{r_{4}}r_{3}^{2}\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r}_{3},t^{\prime})\right\rangle, $$

which can be rewritten as:

$$ \langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle=\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}}\int_{r}^{\infty}\int_{r^{\prime}}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{r_{2}}\int_{0}^{r_{4}}\text{d}r_{1}\text{d}r_{2}\text{d}r_{3}\text{d}r_{4}\left(\frac{r_{1}r_{3}}{r_{2}r_{4}}\right)^{2}\langle\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r}_{1},t)\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r}_{3},t^{\prime})\rangle. $$

Now we similarly divide $\chi(t)$ into contributions:

$$ \langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle=\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}+\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm aniso}_{1}+\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm aniso}_{2}, $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}} \displaystyle\times\int_{r}^{\infty}\int_{r^{\prime}}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{r_{2}}\int_{0}^{r_{4}}\text{d}r_{1}\text{d}r_{2}\text{d}r_{3}\text{d}r_{4}\left(\frac{r_{1}r_{3}}{r_{2}r_{4}}\right)^{2}\langle\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r}_{1},t)\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r}_{3},t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}, $$

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm aniso}_{1}= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}dr\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}} \displaystyle\times\int_{r}^{\infty}\int_{r^{\prime}}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{r_{2}}\int_{0}^{r_{4}}\text{d}r_{1}\text{d}r_{2}\text{d}r_{3}\text{d}r_{4}\left(\frac{r_{1}r_{3}}{r_{2}r_{4}}\right)^{2}\langle\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r}_{1},t)\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r}_{3},t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm aniso}_{1}, $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm aniso}_{2}= \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}} \displaystyle\times\int_{r}^{\infty}\int_{r^{\prime}}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{r_{2}}\int_{0}^{r_{4}}\text{d}r_{1}\text{d}r_{2}\text{d}r_{3}\text{d}r_{4}\left(\frac{r_{1}r_{3}}{r_{2}r_{4}}\right)^{2}\langle\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r}_{1},t)\xi_{R}(\mathbf{r}_{3},t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm aniso}_{2}. $$

We will first solve for $\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}$ . Substitution of Eq. (2.29) into Eq. (2.36) results in:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}= \displaystyle\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}} \displaystyle\times\int_{r}^{\infty}\int_{r^{\prime}}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{r_{2}}\int_{0}^{r_{4}}\text{d}r_{1}\text{d}r_{2}\text{d}r_{3}\text{d}r_{4}\left(\frac{r_{1}r_{3}}{r_{2}r_{4}}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{\partial}{\partial r_{1}}+\frac{2}{r_{1}}\right)\left[\rho(r_{1})\frac{\partial}{\partial r_{1}}\left(\frac{\delta(r_{1}-r_{3})}{r_{1}^{2}}\right)\right]. $$

We now distribute the divergence in $r_{1}$ to find:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}= \displaystyle\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}} \displaystyle\times\int_{r}^{\infty}\int_{r^{\prime}}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{r_{2}}\int_{0}^{r_{4}}\text{d}r_{1}\text{d}r_{2}\text{d}r_{3}\text{d}r_{4}\left(\frac{r_{1}r_{3}}{r_{2}r_{4}}\right)^{2}\frac{\partial}{\partial r_{1}}\left[\rho(r_{1})\frac{\partial}{\partial r_{1}}\left(\frac{\delta(r_{1}-r_{3})}{r_{1}^{2}}\right)\right] \displaystyle+\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}dr\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}} \displaystyle\times\int_{r}^{\infty}\int_{r^{\prime}}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{r_{2}}\int_{0}^{r_{4}}\text{d}r_{1}\text{d}r_{2}\text{d}r_{3}\text{d}r_{4}\left(\frac{r_{3}}{r_{2}r_{4}}\right)^{2}2r_{1}\left[\rho(r_{1})\frac{\partial}{\partial r_{1}}\left(\frac{\delta(r_{1}-r_{3})}{r_{1}^{2}}\right)\right]. $$

We now integrate the top integral by parts, which results in a boundary term as well as an integral which cancels out with the bottom integral. We are then left with:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}= \displaystyle-\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}} \displaystyle\times\int_{r}^{\infty}\int_{r^{\prime}}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{r_{4}}\text{d}r_{2}\text{d}r_{3}\text{d}r_{4}\left(\frac{r_{1}r_{3}}{r_{2}r_{4}}\right)^{2}\left(\rho(r_{1})\frac{\partial}{\partial r_{1}}\left(\frac{\delta(r_{1}-r_{3})}{r_{1}^{2}}\right)\right)\Biggr|^{r_{1}=r_{2}}_{r_{1}=0} $$

Evaluation of the limits must be done with care, particularly for the $r_{1}=0$ term. Before evaluating these limits, we rearrange such that there are no derivatives in $r_{1}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}= \displaystyle\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}} \displaystyle\times\int_{r}^{\infty}\int_{r^{\prime}}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{r_{4}}\text{d}r_{2}\text{d}r_{3}\text{d}r_{4}\left(\frac{r_{3}}{r_{2}r_{4}}\right)^{2}\rho(r_{1})\frac{2}{r_{1}}\delta(r_{1}-r_{3})\Biggr|^{r_{1}=r_{2}}_{r_{1}=0} \displaystyle+\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}} \displaystyle\times\int_{r}^{\infty}\int_{r^{\prime}}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{r_{4}}\text{d}r_{2}\text{d}r_{3}\text{d}r_{4}\left(\frac{r_{3}}{r_{2}r_{4}}\right)^{2}\left(\rho(r_{1})\frac{\partial}{\partial r_{3}}\delta(r_{1}-r_{3})\right)\Biggr|^{r_{1}=r_{2}}_{r_{1}=0}. $$

We now evaluate the limits, noting that the $r_{1}\to 0$ limits will vanish:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}= \displaystyle\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}} \displaystyle\times\int_{r}^{\infty}\int_{r^{\prime}}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{r_{4}}\text{d}r_{2}\text{d}r_{3}\text{d}r_{4}\left(\frac{r_{3}}{r_{2}r_{4}}\right)^{2}\rho(r_{2})\frac{2}{r_{2}}\delta(r_{3}-r_{2}) \displaystyle+\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}} \displaystyle\times\int_{r}^{\infty}\int_{r^{\prime}}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{r_{4}}\text{d}r_{2}\text{d}r_{3}\text{d}r_{4}\left(\frac{r_{3}}{r_{2}r_{4}}\right)^{2}\left(\rho(r_{2})\frac{\partial}{\partial r_{3}}\delta(r_{2}-r_{3})\right). $$

We now integrate the first integral with respect to $r_{3}$ . Because the integral with respect to $r_{3}$ goes from $r_{3}=0$ to $r_{3}=r_{4}$ , the integral will be zero if $r_{4}<r_{2}$ . However, if $r_{4}>r_{2}$ , we can apply the sifting property of the delta function. We can handle both cases by applying the sifting function while applying up a factor of $H(r_{4}-r_{2})$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}= \displaystyle\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}}\int_{r}^{\infty}\int_{r^{\prime}}^{\infty}\text{d}r_{2}\text{d}r_{4}\left(\frac{1}{r_{4}}\right)^{2}\rho(r_{2})\frac{2}{r_{2}}H(r_{4}-r_{2}) \displaystyle+\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}} \displaystyle\times\int_{r}^{\infty}\int_{r^{\prime}}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{r_{4}}\text{d}r_{2}\text{d}r_{3}\text{d}r_{4}\left(\frac{r_{3}}{r_{2}r_{4}}\right)^{2}\left(\rho(r_{2})\frac{\partial}{\partial r_{3}}\delta(r_{2}-r_{3})\right), $$

where $H$ is the Heaviside step function. We can now integrate the bottom integral by parts which results in:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}= \displaystyle\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}}\int_{r}^{\infty}\int_{r^{\prime}}^{\infty}\text{d}r_{2}\text{d}r_{4}\left(\frac{1}{r_{4}}\right)^{2}\rho(r_{2})\frac{2}{r_{2}}H(r_{4}-r_{2}) \displaystyle+\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}} \displaystyle\times\int_{r}^{\infty}\int_{r^{\prime}}^{\infty}\text{d}r_{2}\text{d}r_{4}\left(\frac{r_{3}}{r_{2}r_{4}}\right)^{2}\left(\rho(r_{2})\delta(r_{2}-r_{3})\right)\Biggr|^{r_{3}=r_{4}}_{r_{3}=0} \displaystyle-\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}} \displaystyle\times\int_{r}^{\infty}\int_{r^{\prime}}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{r_{4}}\text{d}r_{2}\text{d}r_{3}\text{d}r_{4}\left(\frac{1}{r_{2}r_{4}}\right)^{2}\left(2r_{3}\rho(r_{2})\delta(r_{2}-r_{3})\right). $$

Evaluate the integral in $r_{3}$ of the bottom integral leads to a term which cancels with the top integral, resulting in:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}= \displaystyle\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}} \displaystyle\times\int_{r}^{\infty}\int_{r^{\prime}}^{\infty}\text{d}r_{2}\text{d}r_{4}\left(\frac{r_{3}}{r_{2}r_{4}}\right)^{2}\left(\rho(r_{2})\delta(r_{2}-r_{3})\right)\Biggr|^{r_{3}=r_{4}}_{r_{3}=0}. $$

We can now evaluate the limits,

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}= \displaystyle\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}}\int_{r}^{\infty}\text{d}r_{2}\left(\frac{1}{r_{2}}\right)^{2}\rho(r_{2})\int_{r^{\prime}}^{\infty}\text{d}r_{4}\delta(r_{2}-r_{4}). $$

Evaluating the integral in $r_{4}$ now depends on $r^{\prime}$ . If $r^{\prime}<r_{2}$ we may apply the sifting property of the delta function. If $r^{\prime}>r_{2}$ the integral vanishes. Therefore we apply the sifting property and gain a factor of the Heaviside step function:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}= \displaystyle\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}}\int_{r}^{\infty}\text{d}r_{2}\left(\frac{1}{r_{2}}\right)^{2}\rho(r_{2})H(r_{2}-r^{\prime}). $$

If $r<r^{\prime}$ then the integral will be zero until $r_{2}$ reaches $r^{\prime}$ . Then we may absorb the step function into the limits of integration:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}= \displaystyle\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}}\int_{\text{max}(r,r^{\prime})}^{\infty}\text{d}r_{2}\left(\frac{1}{r_{2}}\right)^{2}\rho(r_{2}). $$

Integration by parts results in:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}= \displaystyle\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}}\frac{\rho(\text{max}(r,r^{\prime}))}{\text{max}(r,r^{\prime})} \displaystyle+\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}}\int_{\text{max}(r,r^{\prime})}^{\infty}\text{d}r_{2}\left(\frac{1}{r_{2}}\right)\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r_{2}}. $$

The $\text{max}(r,r^{\prime})$ functions are cumbersome to deal with as is. We therefore divide the integrals over $r^{\prime}$ into sections where $r^{\prime}<r$ or $r^{\prime}>r$ :

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}= \displaystyle\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\left(\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{r}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}}\frac{\rho(r)}{r}+\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{r}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}}\frac{\rho(r^{\prime})}{r^{\prime}}\right) \displaystyle+\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{r}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}}\int_{r}^{\infty}\text{d}r_{2}\left(\frac{1}{r_{2}}\right)\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r_{2}} \displaystyle+\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{r}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}}\int_{r^{\prime}}^{\infty}\text{d}r_{2}\left(\frac{1}{r_{2}}\right)\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r_{2}}. $$

We now integrate the last line by parts in $r^{\prime}$ , directly evaluate the integral over $r^{\prime}$ in the second line, and combine like terms. This results in:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}= \displaystyle\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\left(\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{r}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}}\frac{\rho(r)}{r}+\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{r}^{\infty}\text{d}r\text{d}r^{\prime}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r^{\prime}}\frac{\rho(r^{\prime})}{r^{\prime}}\right) \displaystyle-\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\int_{r}^{\infty}\text{d}r_{2}\left(\frac{1}{r_{2}}\right)\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r_{2}} \displaystyle+\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\int_{r}^{\infty}\text{d}r^{\prime}\mathcal{E}\left(\frac{1}{r^{\prime}}\right)\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r^{\prime}}. $$

We now integrate the second integral of the first line by parts and directly evaluate the $r^{\prime}$ integral in the first term of the first line, which results in:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}= \displaystyle\frac{4k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\mathcal{E}\frac{\rho(r)}{r}-\frac{4k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\rho(r)}{r} \displaystyle-\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\int_{r}^{\infty}\text{d}r_{2}\left(\frac{1}{r_{2}}\right)\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r_{2}} \displaystyle+\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\int_{r}^{\infty}\text{d}r^{\prime}\mathcal{E}\left(\frac{1}{r^{\prime}}\right)\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r^{\prime}}. $$

We now integrate both the second and third line by parts, then combine like terms, which results in:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}= \displaystyle\frac{4k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\mathcal{E}\frac{\rho(r)}{r}-\frac{4k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\frac{\rho(r)}{r} \displaystyle+\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\left(\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}\right)^{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\left(\frac{1}{r}\right)\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r}-\frac{4k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\mathcal{E}\left(\frac{1}{r}\right)\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r} \displaystyle+\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\left(\mathcal{E}(r)\right)^{2}\left(\frac{1}{r}\right)\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r}. $$

Now, as was assumed before, we note that each of the above integrals is non-zero only near the interface. Then if $R$ is much larger than the width of the interface, we may rewrite each integral as:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}= \displaystyle\frac{4k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4R\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\mathcal{E}\rho(r)-\frac{4k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4R\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\rho(r) \displaystyle+\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4R\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\left(\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}\right)^{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r}-\frac{4k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4R\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\mathcal{E}\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r} \displaystyle+\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4R\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\left(\mathcal{E}(r)\right)^{2}\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r}+\mathcal{O}(1/R^{2}). $$

The first integral may be rewritten as:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}= \displaystyle\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4R\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left[\left(\mathcal{E}\right)^{2}\right]\rho(r)-\frac{4k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4R\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial r}\rho(r) \displaystyle+\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4R\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\left(\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}\right)^{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r}-\frac{4k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4R\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\mathcal{E}\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r} \displaystyle+\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4R\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\left(\mathcal{E}(r)\right)^{2}\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r}+\mathcal{O}(1/R^{2}). $$

Then the above integrals may be compactly rewritten as:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}= \displaystyle\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4R\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left[\left(\mathcal{E}\right)^{2}\rho(r)\right]-\frac{4k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4R\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left[\mathcal{E}\rho\right] \displaystyle+\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4R\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\left(\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}\right)^{2}\int_{0}^{\infty}\text{d}r\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r}+\mathcal{O}(1/R^{2}). $$

All integrals may now be evaluated directly and simplify to:

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}= \displaystyle\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4R\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\rho^{\rm sat}\left(\mathcal{E}^{\rm sat}-\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}\right)^{2}+\mathcal{O}(1/R^{2}). $$

$\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm aniso}_{1}$ and $\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm aniso}_{2}$ can be solved for in a similar manner as $\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm iso}$ , and we find that $\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm aniso}_{1}$ is zero while $\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm aniso}_{2}$ is:

$$ \langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle^{\rm aniso}_{2}=\frac{4k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4\pi D_{R}\zeta\ell_{o}^{2}R^{2}}\Delta\mathcal{E}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\left[\int_{0}^{\infty}dr\frac{\kappa_{3}(\rho)}{\overline{U}(\rho)}\left(\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r}\right)^{2}\left(\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}-\mathcal{E}\right)\right]+O\left(\frac{1}{R^{3}}\right), $$

which implies that the most significant contributions to the anisotropic noise correlations are $\mathcal{O}(1/R^{2})$ or smaller. Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\langle\chi(t)\chi(t^{\prime})\rangle= \displaystyle\frac{2k_{B}T^{\rm act}}{4R\pi\zeta}\delta(t-t^{\prime})\rho^{\rm sat}\left(\mathcal{E}^{\rm sat}-\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}\right)^{2}+\mathcal{O}(1/R^{2}). $$

We now define $\tilde{\chi}$ as:

$$ \tilde{\chi}(t)=-\frac{\zeta_{\rm eff}}{R\left(\rho^{\rm sat}-\rho^{\rm in}\right)\left(\mathcal{E}^{\rm sat}-\mathcal{E}^{\rm in}\right)}\chi(t), $$

which will have zero mean and correlations:

$$ \langle\tilde{\chi}(t)\tilde{\chi}(t^{\prime})\rangle=2k_{B}T^{\rm act}\zeta_{\rm eff}\delta(t-t^{\prime}). $$

### 2.3 Effective Potential

Cates and Nardini [19] have argued that the nucleation of active matter must have a defineable potential barrier because Eqs. (2.20) and (2.24) satisfy an effective fluctuation dissipation theorem. This nucleation potential is defined such that $F^{D}(R)=-\partial U(R)/\partial R$ :

$$ U(R)=\int\text{d}R8\pi R^{2}\upgamma_{\rm ost}\left[\frac{1}{R}-\frac{1}{R_{C}}\right], $$

where $F^{D}(R)$ is defined by Eq. (2.22). In general, evaluating this integral analytically is difficult because $\upgamma_{\rm ost}$ is implicitly a function of $R$ . Cates and Nardini proposed neglecting the $R$ dependence of $\upgamma_{\rm ost}$ and treating it as a constant:

$$ U(R)=8\pi\upgamma_{\rm ost}\left[\frac{R^{2}}{2}-\frac{R^{3}}{3R_{C}}\right]. $$

We verify the validity of this approximation by evaluating the integrand of Eq. (2.62) both numerically and via the approximation proposed by Cates and Nardini. We follow the same numerical scheme as discussed in Section 1.4, except now $R$ is taken as an input and the two unknown values solved for are $\rho^{\rm in}$ and $\rho^{\rm out}$ . The result of calculating $-\partial U(R)/\partial R$ both from our numerical scheme and the approximation of Cates and Nardini is plotted in Fig. S.2.

*Figure S.2: Deterministic force as defined by the negative derivative in $R$ of Eq. (2.62) as evaluated via the numerical scheme described above or treating coefficients as constant in $R$ . The bubble forces were evaluated for a system at $\ell_{o}/d_{\rm hs}=70.7$ and $R_{C}/d_{\rm hs}=67$ . The droplet forces were evaluated for a system at $\ell_{o}/d_{\rm hs}=70.7$ and $R_{C}/d_{\rm hs}=70$ .*

The difference between ignoring and accounting for the $R$ dependence of $\upgamma_{\rm ost}$ is marginal for both bubbles and droplets, as shown by Fig. S.2. Therefore evaluating coefficients at $R=R_{C}$ and treating them as constant is a robust approximation, justifying the use of Eq. (2.63). We can then define a potential barrier as $U(R_{C})$ , which is given by:

$$ U(R_{C})=\frac{4}{3}\pi\upgamma_{\rm ost}R_{C}^{2}. $$

We use Eq. (2.64) to calculate the nucleation barriers presented in the main text.

We may also substitute $R_{C}$ as defined by Eq. (1.40) into Eq. (2.63) to find a clean separation between terms proportional to surface area and volume:

$$ U(R)=4\pi\upgamma_{\rm ost}R^{2}-\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}\mathcal{V}, $$

where $\mathcal{V}$ has units of energy per volume and has form:

$$ \mathcal{V}=\frac{\mathcal{P}(\rho^{\rm sat})\Delta\rho}{\rho^{\rm sat}}-\frac{\Delta\Phi\Delta\rho}{\rho^{\rm sat}\Delta\mathcal{E}}. $$

### 2.4 Becker-Döring Nucleation Rate Calculation

Using the barriers calculated in the previous Section we can calculate the nucleation rate outlined in Appendix A of the main text, which we reproduce here as:

$$ \mathcal{R}=\left(\rho^{\rm sat}\right)^{2}\pi U_{o}\sqrt{\frac{\upgamma_{\rm ost}}{2\pi(\rho^{\rm in})^{2}k_{B}T^{\rm act}}}\text{exp}\left[-\frac{U(\ell^{*})}{k_{B}T^{\rm act}}\right]. $$

$\mathcal{R}$ is calculated for ABP droplets and the results are plotted in Fig. S.3. At constant $\nu^{\rm sat}$ , while $\upgamma_{\rm ost}/k_{B}T^{\rm act}$ scales roughly linearly with run length, the absolute value of $\rho^{\rm sat}$ also decreases. At constant $\ell_{o}$ , $\rho^{\rm sat}$ increases linearly with $\nu^{\rm sat}$ . These dependencies on activity and saturation within the prefactor are far weaker than the exponential dependence of a barrier which depends strongly on both activity and saturation. Thus the qualitative behavior of Fig. S.3 is dominated by the strength of the nucleation barrier.

## 3 Equilibrium Nucleus Coexistence

In this Section we first derive the finite-sized coexistence of an equilibrium system through a constrained free energy minimization. We then show that a mechanical theory constructed in the same manner as Section 1 is equivalent to equilibrium nucleation theory when the underlying dynamics are passive. For brevity we will skip many steps of the derivation as this procedure will be entirely analogous to those outlined in the previous two Sections.

### 3.1 Thermodynamics of Classical Nucleation

We consider a nucleus of radius $R$ and density $\rho^{\rm in}$ coexisting with a parent phase of density $\rho^{\rm out}$ . The system has an overall density of $\rho^{\rm sat}$ and volume $V$ . The Helmholtz free energy of this system is then given by:

$$ \mathcal{F}=\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}f(\rho^{\rm in})+\left(V-\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}\right)f(\rho^{\rm out})+4\pi R^{2}\upgamma, $$

where $\upgamma$ is the surface tension and $f(\rho)$ is a bulk Helmholtz free energy density of a system with uniform density $\rho$ . The total number of particles in the system is conserved with:

$$ \rho^{\rm in}\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}+\rho^{\rm out}\left(V-\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}\right)=\rho^{\rm sat}V. $$

Our free energy has dependencies on three adjustable internal variables, $\rho^{\rm in}$ , $\rho^{\rm out}$ , and $R$ . The properties associated with a critical nucleus can be found by performing a constrained extremization with respect to $\rho^{\rm in}$ , $\rho^{\rm out}$ , and $R$ and looking for solutions where the radius is finite and not macroscopic. We construct the following Lagrangian:

$$ \mathcal{W}=\mathcal{F}(\rho^{\rm in},\rho^{\rm out},R)-\lambda\left(\rho^{\rm in}\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}+\rho^{\rm out}\left(V-\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}\right)-\rho^{\rm sat}V\right), $$

where $\lambda$ is a Lagrange multiplier. We extremize $\mathcal{W}$ by setting its partial derivatives with respect to $\rho^{\rm in}$ , $\rho^{\rm out}$ , $\lambda$ , and $R$ (and evaluating these variables at their unknown critical values) to zero:

$$ \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=\frac{\partial\mathcal{W}}{\partial\rho^{\rm in}}\Bigr|_{\rho^{\rm in}=\rho^{\rm in*}}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial\rho}\Bigr|_{\rho=\rho^{\rm in^{*}}}-\lambda^{*}, \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=\frac{\partial\mathcal{W}}{\partial\rho^{\rm out}}\Bigr|_{\rho^{\rm out}=\rho^{\rm out*}}=\frac{\partial f}{\partial\rho}\Bigr|_{\rho=\rho^{\rm out^{*}}}-\lambda^{*}, \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=\frac{\partial\mathcal{W}}{\partial R}\Bigr|_{R=R_{C}}=f(\rho^{\rm in})-f(\rho^{\rm out})-\lambda^{*}\left(\rho^{\rm in}-\rho^{\rm out}\right)+\frac{2\upgamma}{R_{C}}, \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=\frac{\partial\mathcal{W}}{\partial\lambda}\Bigr|_{\lambda=\lambda^{*}}=(\rho^{\rm in}-\rho^{\rm out})\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}+(\rho^{\rm out}-\rho^{\rm sat})V. $$

Here $\rho^{\rm in*}$ , $\rho^{\rm out*}$ , $\lambda^{*}$ , and $R_{C}$ denote the extremized values of $\rho^{\rm in}$ , $\rho^{\rm out}$ , $\lambda$ , and $R$ , respectively. Defining the chemical potential as $\mu(\rho)\equiv\partial f/\partial\rho$ allows us to appreciate that the extremized value of the Lagrange multiplier, $\lambda^{*}$ , is simply the coexistence chemical potential with $\lambda^{*}\equiv\mu^{\rm coexist}=\mu(\rho^{\rm in*})=\mu(\rho^{\rm out*})$ by combining Eqs. (3.4a) and (3.4b). By defining the thermodynamic pressure, $p(\rho)\equiv-f(\rho)+\rho\mu(\rho)$ , we can express the coexistence criteria with the following three equations:

$$ \displaystyle\mu(\rho^{\rm in*}) \displaystyle=\mu(\rho^{\rm out*}), \displaystyle p(\rho^{\rm in*}) \displaystyle=p(\rho^{\rm out*})+\frac{2\upgamma}{R_{C}}, \displaystyle\rho^{\rm sat}V \displaystyle=\rho^{\rm in*}\frac{4}{3}\pi R_{C}^{3}+\rho^{\rm out*}\left(V-\frac{4}{3}\pi R_{C}^{3}\right). $$

Equations (3.5) allow for the determination of the unknown densities and critical radius.

As we are interested in solutions in which the radius takes on large but non-macroscopic values, we consider the limit of $R^{3}\ll V$ . In this limit, the particle conservation equation [Eq. (3.2)] reduces to $\rho^{\rm out}\approx\rho^{\rm sat}$ and the nucleus in contact with a infinite particle reservoir with chemical potential $\mu(\rho^{\rm sat})\equiv\mu^{\rm sat}$ . The Lagrangian then takes the following form:

$$ \mathcal{W}\approx\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}\left(w(\rho^{\rm in})-w(\rho^{\rm sat})\right)+4\pi R^{2}\upgamma, $$

where $w(\rho)\equiv f(\rho)-\mu^{\rm sat}\rho$ is the grand potential energy density (also equivalent to the negative pressure, $-p$ ) of a system with density $\rho$ in contact with a particle reservoir with chemical potential $\mu^{\rm sat}$ . We can plainly identify that the simplified Lagrangian contains two familiar terms in classical nucleation theory: a negative volumetric term proportional to the grand potential energy density difference between the nucleus and the parent phase and positive areal term proportional to the surface tension. The volumetric driving term defined in the main text [i.e., ${\mathcal{W}=-\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}\mathcal{V}+4\pi R^{2}\upgamma}$ ] has several equivalent forms ${\mathcal{V}\equiv-\Delta w\equiv\Delta p\equiv-\Delta f+\mu^{\rm sat}\Delta\rho}$ where we have again used the notation of ${\Delta a=a(\rho^{\rm in})-a(\rho^{\rm sat})}$ . Extremization of $\mathcal{W}$ with respect to $R$ and $\rho^{\rm in}$ results in the following coexistence criteria:

$$ \displaystyle\mu(\rho^{\rm in*}) \displaystyle=\mu^{\rm sat}, \displaystyle p(\rho^{\rm in*}) \displaystyle=p(\rho^{\rm sat})+\frac{2\upgamma}{R_{C}}. R_{C}\ll V F^{{\dagger}}\equiv\mathcal{W}(\rho^{\rm in}=\rho^{\rm in*},R=R_{C}) R_{C} \displaystyle R_{C} \displaystyle=\frac{2\upgamma}{w(\rho^{\rm sat})-w(\rho^{\rm in*})}. $$

We note that in the main text and for most of this SI we denote $\rho^{\rm in*}$ simply as $\rho^{\rm in}$ for notational convenience. The stability of the solutions to Eqs. (3.7) can be determined by computing the Hessian matrix of $\mathcal{W}$ and evaluating it at the solutions. A positive surface energy and volumetric driving force for growth will generally result in the critical nucleus representing a unstable fixed point.

### 3.2 Equilibrium Density Field

We consider particles which follow an overdamped Langevin equation with an additional translational Brownian stochastic noise that satisfies the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. The overdamped Langevin equation for the $i$ th particle of this system is:

$$ \displaystyle\dot{\mathbf{r}}_{i}=\frac{1}{\zeta}\sum_{j\neq i}^{N}\mathbf{F}_{ij}+\bm{\eta}_{i}(t), $$

where $\bm{\eta}_{i}$ is the translational Brownian noise with zero average and variance $\langle\bm{\eta}_{i}(t)\bm{\eta}_{j}(t^{\prime})=2(k_{B}T/\zeta)\delta(t-t^{\prime})\delta_{ij}\mathbf{I}\rangle$ . For this system to be passive, we require that the interparticle forces $\mathbf{F}_{ij}$ are reciprocal, i.e. $\mathbf{F}_{ij}=-\mathbf{F}_{ji}$ . We assume that the interparticle forces, overall system density, and temperature are such that the system is phase separated. Following the Irving-Kirkwood-Noll [5, 7] procedure for a system described by Eq. (3.8) results in the following density field dynamics at the mean-field level:

$$ \displaystyle\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t} \displaystyle=-\bm{\nabla}\cdot\mathbf{J},\  \displaystyle\mathbf{J} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\zeta}\bm{\nabla}\cdot\left(\bm{\sigma}^{C}+\bm{\sigma}^{B}\right),\  \displaystyle\bm{\sigma}^{C} \displaystyle=\left[-p_{C}(\rho)+\rho\kappa(\rho)\nabla^{2}\rho+\frac{\left(\kappa(\rho)+\rho\frac{\partial\kappa}{\partial\rho}\right)}{2}|\bm{\nabla}\rho|^{2}\right]\mathbf{I}-\kappa(\rho)\bm{\nabla}\rho\bm{\nabla}\rho,\  \displaystyle\bm{\sigma}^{B} \displaystyle=-k_{B}T\rho\mathbf{I},\  $$

where $\bm{\sigma}^{B}$ is the “ideal gas” stress generated by the stochastic translational Brownian noise (absent in our treatment of athermal active matter) and we define $p(\rho)=p_{C}(\rho)+k_{B}T\rho$ . We also note that in this model of equilibrium dynamics the stress tensor is fully local.

Within these passive dynamics we may identify ${\kappa_{1}(\rho)=\rho\kappa(\rho)}$ , ${\kappa_{2}(\rho)=1/2\left(\rho\partial\kappa/\partial\rho+\kappa(\rho)\right)}$ , ${\kappa_{3}(\rho)=-\kappa(\rho)}$ , and ${\kappa_{4}(\rho)=0}$ . This result was first identified by Korteweg [13], and these relations have been demonstrated as equivalent to assuming variational dynamics of some Ginzburg-Landau free energy functional [22]. In this case Eq. (1.17) reduces to:

$$ \frac{\partial^{2}\mathcal{E}}{\partial\rho^{2}}=-\frac{1}{\rho}\frac{\partial\mathcal{E}}{\partial\rho} $$

In this case, (within inconsequential constants of integration,) the identity of the pseudovariable becomes $\mathcal{E}\sim 1/\rho=v$ , the molecular volume. By substituting Eq. (3.9) into Eq. (1.9), we may simplify the mechanical surface tension to:

$$ \upgamma_{\rm mech}=\int_{0}^{\infty}dr\mathcal{G}(\rho)=\int_{0}^{\infty}dr\kappa(\rho)\left(\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r}\right)^{2}. $$

By substituting $\mathcal{E}=1/\rho$ into Eq. (1.23), we may simplify the Ostwald tension to:

$$ \displaystyle\upgamma_{\rm ost} \displaystyle=\frac{v^{\rm sat}\left(\rho^{\rm sat}-\rho^{\rm in}\right)}{\left(v^{\rm sat}-v^{\rm in}\right)}\left[\int_{0}^{\infty}\left(-\rho\kappa(\rho)\frac{1}{\rho^{2}}\left(\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r}\right)^{2}+\kappa(\rho)\left(\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{1}{\rho}-v^{\rm in}\right)\right)\text{d}r\right], \displaystyle=-\frac{v^{\rm sat}v^{\rm in}\left(\rho^{\rm sat}-\rho^{\rm in}\right)}{\left(v^{\rm sat}-v^{\rm in}\right)}\left[\int_{0}^{\infty}\kappa(\rho)\left(\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r}\right)^{2}\text{d}r\right], \displaystyle=-\frac{\left(v^{\rm in}\rho^{\rm sat}-1\right)}{\left(1-\rho^{\rm sat}v^{\rm in}\right)}\left[\int_{0}^{\infty}\kappa(\rho)\left(\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r}\right)^{2}\text{d}r\right], \displaystyle=\int_{0}^{\infty}\kappa(\rho)\left(\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial r}\right)^{2}\text{d}r=\upgamma_{\rm mech}, $$

where we have used $v=1/\rho$ . Therefore the equilibrium Ostwald tension is identical to the equilibrium mechanical surface tension.

We now discuss the equilibrium relationship between $\mathcal{E}$ and the AMB+ pseudovaribale $\psi$ in order to avoid any potential confusion. As discussed in Section 1.7, AMB+ can be mapped to the divergence of some dynamic stress tensor $\bm{\Sigma}$ , with the mapping dependent on the choice of mobility $M[\rho]$ . Choosing $M[\rho]=\rho$ and setting the nonequilibrium AMB+ constants $(\lambda,\mathcal{Z})$ will result in a $\bm{\Sigma}$ that exactly recovers the Korteweg stress tensor from Eq. (3.9). This mapping also results in $\psi\sim\rho$ . One may also deduce that $\psi\sim\rho$ from Section 1.7 after noting that the choice of $M[\rho]=\rho$ is an instance of the $M[\rho]\sim 1/\mathcal{E}$ case already discussed in detail.

### 3.3 Equivalence of Thermodynamic and Mechanical Perspectives

We now demonstrate that the mechanically-derived generalized critical nucleus criteria [Eqs. (1.25) and (1.24)] applied to passive systems recover the criteria obtained through the variational method described in Section 3.1. The pseudovariable variable for passive systems [11, 1] is simply $\mathcal{E}\sim v$ where $v=1/\rho$ is the specific volume and the equivalence of the Ostwald and mechanical tensions $\upgamma_{\rm ost}=\upgamma_{\rm mech}\equiv\upgamma$ results in the generalized criteria now taking the following form for passive systems:

$$ p(\rho^{\rm in})-p(\rho^{\rm sat})=\frac{2\upgamma}{R_{C}}, \int_{v^{\rm in}}^{v^{\rm sat}}\left[p(v)-p(v^{\rm sat})\right]\text{d}v+\frac{2\upgamma v^{\rm in}}{R_{C}}=0, $$

where we have also recognized that the dynamic pressure is simply the static thermodynamic pressure. Eq. (3.13a) is the familiar Laplace pressure difference criterion that was recovered in Section 3.1 using thermodynamics. All that is required to establish the equivalence of the criteria obtained from our mechanical approach [Eqs. (3.13)] and the thermodynamically obtained criteria [Eqs. (3.7)] is to demonstrate the equivalence of Eq. (3.13b) with equality of chemical potential. We first eliminate the surface tension from Eq. (3.13b) by using the Laplace pressure difference, resulting in:

$$ \int_{v^{\rm in}}^{v^{\rm sat}}p(v)dv-\left(p(v^{\rm sat})v^{\rm sat}-p(v^{\rm in})v^{\rm in}\right)=0. $$

Integration by parts demonstrates that the left-hand-side of the above equation is simply $\int_{p^{\rm in}}^{p^{\rm sat}}vdp$ , which is equivalent to $\int_{\mu^{\rm in}}^{\mu^{\rm sat}}d\mu$ via the Gibbs-Duhem relation, $vdp=d\mu$ . We thus arrive at the expected:

$$ \mu(\rho^{\rm in})=\mu^{\rm sat}, $$

demonstrating the equivalence of our mechanically derived criteria with those derived from thermodynamic considerations.

In Section 2.3 we identified a general expression for the volumetric contribution to the effective nucleation barrier:

$$ \mathcal{V}=\frac{\mathcal{P}(\rho^{\rm sat})\Delta\rho}{\rho^{\rm sat}}-\frac{\Delta\Phi\Delta\rho}{\rho^{\rm sat}\Delta\mathcal{E}}. $$

With $\Phi=\int pd\mathcal{E}$ and again noting $\upgamma_{\rm ost}=\upgamma_{\rm mech}\equiv\upgamma$ and $\mathcal{E}\sim v$ , one can straightforwardly show:

$$ \mathcal{V}=\mu^{\rm sat}\Delta\rho-\Delta f=-\Delta w. $$

Therefore the mechanical theory recovers the expected thermodynamic driving force for nucleation found in Eq. (3.6).

### 3.4 Application to van der Waals Fluid

Let us consider an equilibrium system where $\kappa(\rho)$ is a constant and $p(\rho)$ is given by the van der Waals equation of state:

$$ \left(p+\rho^{2}a\right)\left(\frac{1}{\rho}-b\right)=k_{B}T, $$

where $a$ is a measure of the average attraction between molecules and $b$ is the volume excluded by a single particle. The critical point of this system is given by:

$$ p^{C}=\frac{a}{27b^{2}},\quad k_{B}T^{C}=\frac{8a}{27b},\quad\rho^{C}=\frac{1}{3b}. $$

We now non-dimensionalize variables by their value at the critical point:

$$ p^{\prime}=\frac{p}{p^{C}},\quad T^{\prime}=\frac{T}{T^{C}},\quad\rho^{\prime}=\frac{\rho}{\rho^{C}}. $$

Then the dimensionless van der Waals equation of state is given by:

$$ p^{\prime}=\frac{8T^{\prime}}{\frac{3}{\rho^{\prime}}-1}-3(\rho^{\prime})^{2}. $$

Equation (3.20) results in the following dimensionless form of $\kappa$ :

$$ \kappa^{\prime}=\kappa\frac{\left(\rho^{C}\right)^{8/3}}{p^{C}} $$

We note that this non-dimensionalized form of the van der Waals equation of state leads to two different natural energy scales: $k_{B}T^{C}$ and $p^{C}/\rho^{C}$ . When calculating the mechanical surface tension of a phase separated Van der Waals fluid via Eq. (1.9), our above non-dimensionalization results in the latter energy scale. In order to convert it to have units of $k_{B}T^{C}$ one can simply multiply the final result by a factor of $3/8$ .

We now set $\kappa^{\prime}=1$ and calculate the coexisting density and radius of the critical nuclei for van der Waals fluids. This calculation was carried out similarly to those done for the active nuclei, only now with the van der Waals equation of state. The results of this calculation are plotted in Fig. S.4.

*Figure S.4: Critical radius and relative change in nucleus density ( $\nu^{\rm in}\equiv|\rho^{\rm in}-\rho^{\rm gas,\rm liq}|/\rho^{\rm gas,\rm liq}$ ) as a function of supersaturation ( $\nu^{\rm sat}\equiv|\rho^{\rm sat}-\rho^{\rm gas,\rm liq}|/\rho^{\rm gas,\rm liq}$ ).*

In addition, we may calculate the nucleation barrier as a function of saturation and temperature using Eq. (2.64), noting that $\upgamma_{\rm ost}=\upgamma_{\rm mech}$ for this passive system. The results of this calculation are plotted in Fig. S.5.

## 4 Active Coarsening Numerics

In this Section we report numerical results for the coarsening of a highly dilute ABP system, using the numerical method outlined in Appendix C, demonstrating the recovery of LSW theory [23].

Given the periodic cell dimensions, nucleus locations, and nucleus radii, it is straightforward to set up the necessary matrix equations to find the coarsening rates and numerically integrate. We conduct numerical simulation of periodic cells of 250 nuclei radii randomly drawn from a distribution. The PACKMOL software package [24] was used to give random locations within the periodic cells such that all nuclei had a separation of at least two times the largest radius. Particle sizes were sampled such that they had an average radius of $750d_{\rm hs}$ and a cubic cell of width $a_{o}=2.1\times 10^{5}d_{\rm hs}$ , corresponding to an overall volume fraction of $2\times 10^{-7}$ . For the overall phase fractions simulated, we expect the results of LSW theory [23] to be recovered. The main predictions of LSW theory are the average nucleus size growing with the cube root of time and a steady-state distribution of nucleus sizes $P(R)\propto\mathcal{N}(x)$ at long times, where $x$ is the ratio of the nucleus radius to the average nucleus radius and $\mathcal{N}$ is proportional to:

$$ \begin{cases}x^{2}(3+x)^{-7/3}\left(\frac{3}{2}-x\right)^{-11/3}\text{exp}\left(-\frac{3}{3-2x}\right)&x<3/2\\
0&x\geq 3/2.\end{cases} $$

We therefore initialized all simulations with radii sampled from a Gaussian distribution as well as initial radii sampled from the distribution predicted by LSW. Simulations were integrated in time for a duration of $6\times 10^{8}d_{hs}/U_{o}$ . Simulation results were averaged over 10 independent randomly generated initial positions and radii for both of the intial distributions. We plot the average nucleus radius cubed as a function of time in Figs. S.6 and S.7.

*Figure S.6: Average radius growth as a function of time for nuclei intialized with a Gaussian distribution with mean $750d_{\rm hs}$ .*

*Figure S.7: Average radius growth as a function of time for nuclei initialized with an LSW distribution with mean $750d_{\rm hs}$ .*

Growth rates demonstrate excellent agreement with the scaling predicted by LSW theory. Droplets coarsen significantly faster than bubbles due to the higher $\upgamma_{\rm ost}$ and therefore larger driving force for coarsening. The distribution of nucleus sizes was also measured in the final third of the simulation time (i.e. times from $4-6\times 10^{8}$ ) and are given by Figs. S.8 and S.9.

*Figure S.8: Nucleus size distribution sampled from last third of simulation steps for particles initialized with Gaussian distribution.*

*Figure S.9: Nucleus size distribution sampled from last third of simulation steps for particles initialized with LSW distribution.*

The nuclei initialized from Gaussian distribution veer from their initial sampling significantly by the end of the simulation time while nuclei initialized from the LSW distribution stay close to the LSW distribution, although with some error due to the finite amount of sampling.
